# Choosing Adhesives for Re-attaching a Detached Side Mirror Housing

When a plastic mirror surface separates from its housing, it feels like a simple cosmetic failure, but selecting the right adhesive is actually an engineering problem involving material science and structural integrity. The issue isn't just "gluing" two pieces together; it's about bonding dissimilar polymers that have likely been exposed to temperature extremes, UV radiation, and mechanical vibration over time.

The core challenge here is the difference between the mirror glass (often mounted on a rigid backing) and the side mirror housing, which is almost exclusively made of high-impact polystyrene or ABS plastic. A standard household glue like super glue or generic cyanoacrylate will fail quickly in this scenario. These adhesives cure by releasing heat when moisture contacts them, creating strong bonds that are brittle and lack flexibility. Once your car hits a pothole or the temperature drops significantly, the housing contracts at a different rate than the cured adhesive, causing the bond to snap.

For re-attachment, you need an adhesive with specific properties: high tensile strength for plastic-to-plastic bonding, excellent UV resistance, and thermal flexibility. The industry standard for automotive exterior applications is usually a two-part urethane structural adhesive or a specialized polyurethane formulation designed for automotive trim. These products remain slightly flexible after curing, allowing the housing to expand and contract with the vehicle body without shattering the bond line.

### Surface Preparation: The Critical Step

Before applying any adhesive, the success of the repair depends entirely on surface preparation. If you rush this step, even the best structural glue will fail within weeks. You must remove all traces of old adhesive, wax, silicone, and oxidation from both the mirror housing flange and the back of the plastic mirror face.

Use a solvent like isopropyl alcohol or acetone to degrease the surfaces. Acetone works well for breaking down old polyurethane residues but requires caution as it can soften certain plastics if left too long. Once cleaned, lightly abrade the mating surfaces with fine-grit sandpaper (around 220 grit). This mechanical roughening increases the surface area and provides a "key" for the adhesive to grip onto. Wipe away all dust immediately after sanding; any particulate matter trapped under the new glue will create stress points that lead to delamination.

### Application Strategy and Curing Time

When applying the adhesive, avoid using too much material. Excessive glue creates long bond lines that are prone to cracking because they cannot flex uniformly during thermal cycling. Instead, apply a thin, consistent bead along the perimeter of the housing where it meets the mirror face. Fill any gaps with just enough compound to ensure full contact, but do not overfill.

Press the components together firmly and align them precisely before the adhesive reaches its initial set time. Most structural urethanes have a working time of 5 to 10 minutes. Use masking tape or temporary clamps to hold the mirror in place during this window. It is crucial to follow the manufacturer's full cure time, which often ranges from 24 to 72 hours for maximum strength. Driving on the car before the adhesive has fully cured can compromise the bond permanently due to vibration and stress loads.

### Trade-offs and Limitations

There are inherent limitations to re-attaching a broken mirror housing. Even with the best adhesive, you cannot restore the original factory seal against water intrusion. The new bond line may eventually allow moisture to seep behind the glass if the fit isn't perfect or if the adhesive settles over time. This could lead to fogging inside the housing or corrosion of internal mechanisms if they are accessible.

Additionally, color matching remains a significant challenge. While clear urethane adhesives are available, they often discolor over time when exposed to sunlight, leaving a visible dark line around the perimeter of the mirror. If aesthetics matter as much as function, consider whether replacing the entire assembly is more cost-effective than managing these visual trade-offs.
